chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 21 to 30, the crab decade of the marutham hundred: ten four- and five-line poems in which the friend asks the mother, each time ending எவன்கொல் அன்னாய், why the girl pales and wastes for the man of the field town, while the field crab cuts lilies, creepers, sprouts and paddy, abandons its mate or hoards in its hole as the figure of what he does.

21.reading: The friend asks the mother why, although the man of the cool-ford town, where the speckled crab cuts the water lily on the banks of old water overgrown with mulli, gives his assurances, the girl's darkened eyes still turn pale.
21.nuance: The whole poem turns on the concession in தெளிப்பவும், 'even as he assures': the pallor answers his words and contradicts them. The crab cutting the lily can be felt as the ooran harming the girl, but the scene offers only that one correspondence, so it is left as scene (a near miss for ullurai).

thinai_evidence.note: the field crab, the water lily and the man named as lord of a watered town

22.reading: The friend asks the mother why the man of the town where the speckled crab, having wallowed in the mire, goes back into its hole at the mulli's roots, after speaking fair words and joining her, said that now he would never leave her.
22.nuance: நீயேன் is read as the negative first person of நீ, 'I will not leave'; the question is then why he made a promise his conduct now belies. The crab's return to its own hole after the mud can be read as the man going back to his own house after his pleasures, but only that one match holds, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: mire, field crab and the lord of a town

comparisons.tenor: the man who assured and embraced her, now the cause of her affliction

23.reading: The friend asks why the man of the town adorned by floodwater, which stirred the crab out of its hole in the mulli roots and came on plucking flowers, having given his assurance and joined with us, should now become a goddess that strikes.
23.nuance: தாக்கணங்கு, a deity that strikes those who approach it, is the word for what the lover has become: the one who should heal is now the cause of the sickness, which is why the friend speaks to the mother, who would otherwise look for the god. நப், 'us', joins the friend to the girl.

thinai_evidence.note: flood, field crab and the lord of a watered town

comparisons.vehicle: தாய்சாப் பிறக்கும் புள்ளிக் களவனொடு பிள்ளை தின்னும் முதலைத்து அவனூர்
comparisons.tenor: the husband who takes the beauty of the women he embraced and abandons them

24.reading: The friend asks whether the husband has come to share the nature of his town, the town of the speckled crab whose birth kills its mother and of the crocodile that eats its own young, since he takes the beauty of the women he embraced till their gold bangles rang and then abandons them.
24.nuance: The two creatures are both kin-destroyers, the young that kill the parent and the parent that eats the young, so the friend charges the man with destroying those who are his own. Because she states the link (அவனூர் எய்தினன் ஆகின்று கொல்லோ), it is an open juxtaposition, not ullurai.

thinai_evidence.note: crab and crocodile of the fields and the husband named மகிழ்நன்

ullurai.tenor: the ooran and the young women of other houses he spoils

pairs.situation: the man cuts short the bloom of the women he takes
the women are of other houses, not his own
they are young girls just coming into growth

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a field crab and a yard creeper of the marutham town, without leaving the poem's land (porul 7.27)

25.reading: The friend tells the mother that the chest of the man of the field town, where the crab cuts the red stem of the vayalai creeper, with its fresh young green pods, that has spread over from the neighbouring yard, brings bangle-loosening grief to many women.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's chest is shared among many women, in a town of fields

ullurai.tenor: the ooran who leaves his own woman and harms others

pairs.situation: he leaves the woman who is his partner
he goes on to hurt other tender women

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the crab and vallai of the marutham field, without leaving the poem's land (porul 7.27)

26.reading: The friend asks the mother why the man of the town where, in a karanthai-grown field, the crab leaves its mate and cuts the soft stalks of the vallai, cares for neither us nor the other women, and has become such a man.
26.nuance: The karanthai here is the field plant, not the puram thinai of the same name. The crab's abandoning its mate is also an act a person of the situation does, but it is the same carrier as the ullurai, so no iraicchi is tagged.

thinai_evidence.note: a field, its crab and the water creeper vallai

ullurai.tenor: the ooran who takes the girl's beauty and keeps to his own house

pairs.situation: he takes the ripe bloom of the girl
he withdraws with it into his own home and does not come back

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the crab and paddy of the marutham field, without leaving the poem's land (porul 7.27)

27.reading: The friend asks why, because of the man of the town where the crab carries off an ear of grain from the red-paddy field into its cool earthen hole, the girl, her bright bangles slipping and her body wasted, labours in grief.

thinai_evidence.note: red paddy field and its crab

28.reading: The friend tells the mother that if this lingering sickness were the work of the goddess of the drinking ford it would be one thing, but asks why, for the man of the town where the crab scores lines in the cool mud, the girl's soft shoulders turn pale as her bright bangles slip and she wastes.
28.nuance: The friend names the cure the mother would seek (the goddess of the ford) in order to set it aside: the cause is a man, and that is the disclosure the poem makes. The opening conditional is compressed and its construction is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the drinking ford, cool mud and its crab

ullurai.tenor: the girl guarded by her family and the ooran who reached her

pairs.situation: her people have raised and watched over the girl
the man cuts off her young bloom, which turns to pallor

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the sown field, its watchmen and its crab, things of the marutham land (porul 7.27)

29.reading: The friend asks the mother why your daughter, with the spotted loins, takes on pallor after she came close to the chest of the man of the field town, where the crab cuts the white sprouts that the watchmen sowed in haste when the rains set in.

30.reading: The friend asks why, because of the man of the town where the crab with long eyes like neem buds fills its cool earthen hole with the large flowers of the paddy, this girl loses her great beauty.
30.nuance: The crab's hole is filled while the girl is emptied of beauty; the contrast is felt but only the one match (his gain, her loss) holds, so it is scene, a near miss for ullurai.

links.note: Both turn on assurance (தெளிப்பவும், தெளித்தசொல்): in Ainkurunuru 21 the friend sets the man's assurances against the girl's paling eyes; in Kural 1154 the woman asks whether those who trusted the assuring word are at fault if he leaves.
links.teaches: The Kural asks who bears the blame once a trusted promise fails, while the Ainkurunuru shows the body already failing while the promise is still being spoken, so the couplet's moral question comes after a doubt that the older poem places in the girl's eyes before any leaving.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 24 says he takes the beauty (நலங்கொண்டு) of the women he embraced and abandons them; Kural 1183 says he took her grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor in exchange.
links.teaches: The Kural turns the friend's accusation of plain taking into an exchange in which pallor is the payment, so the same loss that the Sangam friend calls the act of a kin-destroying creature becomes, in the couplet, the woman's own bitter bookkeeping.

links.note: Both use the belief that the crab is killed by its own young: Ainkurunuru 24 names the crab born at its mother's death (தாய்சாப் பிறக்கும்), Sirupanchamoolam 10 lists its own brood as death to the crab (ஞெண்டிற்குத் தன்பார்ப்பு).
links.teaches: The pairing shows a piece of field lore surviving from the akam landscape into the didactic list: the Sangam friend uses it to charge a man with destroying his own, while the later moralist uses it to say a thing's own offspring or speech is its death, so the same belief turned from accusation of another into warning to oneself.

links.note: Both say the man's chest belongs to many women: Ainkurunuru 25's friend says the ooran's chest (மார்புபலர்க்கு) brings grief to many; Kural 1311's wife refuses his chest (மார்பு) because all women feast on it with their eyes.
links.teaches: The friend counts the cost to the many women his chest has harmed, while the Kural wife refuses that chest because it is shared even by looks, so held together they show the same charge of a common chest used first as report to the mother and then as the wife's own ground for refusal.

links.note: Both mark the loss in the shoulders and the slipping bangle: Ainkurunuru 28 has the bright bangle loosening as the soft shoulders pale (ஒண்டொடி நெகிழ, மென் தோள் பசப்பது); Kural 1234 has the bangle slipping from shoulders that have lost their old beauty.
links.teaches: The Ainkurunuru friend uses the paled shoulders to tell the mother that a man, not the ford goddess, is the cause, while the Kural keeps only the signs, so the couplet's portrait of wasting shoulders was in the older poem a piece of evidence in a disclosure.

links.note: Both open on the neem-bud-eyed crab of the marutham field and its earthen hole (வேப்புநனை யன்ன நெடுங்கள் களவன், வேப்புநனை அன்ன நெடுங்கண் நீர்ஞெண்டு, மண்அளை): in Ainkurunuru 30 it fills its hole with paddy blossom while the girl loses her beauty; in Akananuru 176 it flees the heron into its hole in a poem refusing the husband at the door.
links.teaches: The neem-bud simile and the crab's earthen hole are a shared marutham formula, and the two poems make it mean opposite things by the act they give it, hoarding in the four-line poem and fearful hiding in the long one, so in this stock image the sense lies in what the crab does, not in how it looks.

source_issues: The colophons give no thurai for this decade; every thurai_akam (the friend speaking to the foster mother, அன்னாய்) is inferred from the poems (நின்மகள் in 29, இவள் in 28 and 30), and occasion stage and words are left null.
30 line 1 reads நெடுங்கள் களவன்; the same formula in Akananuru 176 line 8 reads நெடுங்கண், and 'long-eyed' is the sense, so நெடுங்கள் is probably a misprint for நெடுங்கண்; marked as written.
The decade title is கள்வன் பத்து while the repaired lines read களவன்; both spellings of the crab are in use and the poems are marked as written.
22 line 4 நீயேன் is read as 'I will not leave'; the verse is marked uncertain.
24 lines 2-3 (முதலைத்து அவனூர் எய்தினன் ஆகின்று கொல்லோ) are compressed and the construction is uncertain; line 3 is the tamilvu.org reading flagged by show.
28 line 1 (உண்துறை அணங்கிவள் உறைநோய் ஆயின்) is a compressed conditional; the verse is marked uncertain.
23 line 2 prints அணி யூரன் split; read as அணியூரன்.
